text:
The cyberpunk metropolis, a sprawling vertical labyrinth of steel and glass, pulsed with an artificial vitality that never slept. Its skyline was a jagged constellation of light, where skyscrapers pierced the smog-choked sky, their facades draped in cascading waterfalls of neon advertisements. These digital billboards, omnipresent and unblinking, cast a sickly pink and electric blue glow over the streets below, turning the perpetual night into a kaleidoscope of commercial desire.

Beneath this luminous canopy, the city thrummed with the mechanical heartbeat of hovercars, their anti-grav engines humming a low, constant drone that vibrated through the pavement. The streets were a churning river of humanity—corporate elites in tailored synth-silk weaving through crowds of laborers in worn-out tech-wear, all moving with the frantic urgency of a society addicted to speed and connection. The air was thick with the scent of ozone, fried street food, and the metallic tang of recycled rainwater.

In this high-tech, low-life environment, the concept of a candle is an archaic relic, a stark contrast to the electric omnipresence above. The primary material of a traditional candle is wax, a solid hydrocarbon mixture derived from tallow, beeswax, or, in modern synthetic iterations, paraffin or soy. In this neon-drenched world, such a simple object would be a profound anomaly. Its wax would be a remnant of a pre-digital age, a material that burns not with the cold efficiency of LED or the chaotic flicker of holograms, but with a warm, organic, and fleeting flame. It would stand as a silent testament to a time when light was something you had to create and maintain, rather than something that was constantly projected onto your retinas by corporate algorithms.
